opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the resistance is quite revealing. When you ask these companies whether they can guarantee that their systems won't, say, help someone build a biological weapon, or won't attempt to escape from their environment, or won't manipulate users, the honest answer is that they can't, because they don't understand how the systems work. These are giant black boxes. We train trillions of parameters through essentially random perturbations, and what comes out is something whose internal principles of operation are a mystery even to the people who built it.

So when they say "it's not possible to provide guarantees," in a sense they're telling the truth. But the conclusion they draw is the wrong one. They conclude that therefore no one should ask for guarantees. The conclusion any other industry would draw is that therefore you shouldn't be deploying the product.

Think about nuclear power. If a company came to the regulator and said, "We'd like to build a reactor next to a city, but we can't really tell you what the probability of a meltdown is, because we don't understand the physics inside the core," the regulator wouldn't say, "Oh well, that's fine then, go ahead." They would say, "Come back when you do understand it." The nuclear industry has to show that the probability of a major accident is below something like one in ten million per reactor-year. Aircraft, medicines, the same principle applies. The burden of proof is on the developer.

What we've seen with AI is an inversion of that. The companies have essentially said, "The technology is the way it is, and it's up to you to prove it's dangerous before you can stop us." And they've been quite effective in lobbying for that position, often with the argument that any regulation will stifle innovation or let China win.

I'd also point out that there's a contradiction in their stance. Many of the leaders of these companies have themselves said publicly that the technology poses a risk of human extinction, and some have put numbers on it, ten, twenty, twenty-five percent. If you genuinely believe that what you're building has a one-in-five chance of ending the human race, then refusing to accept any requirement to demonstrate safety is extraordinary. No one gave them permission to play Russian roulette with every person on Earth.

So I interpret the resistance partly as an admission that the current technology simply isn't amenable to safety guarantees, and partly as a commercial calculation that it's cheaper to fight regulation than to do the hard work of building systems that are provably safe. My view is that we need to flip the default: red lines on behaviors that are clearly unacceptable, such as self-replication, breaking into other computer systems, or advising terrorists on weapons, and a requirement that developers demonstrate with high confidence that their systems won't cross those lines. If that means the current approach to building AI doesn't qualify, then we need a different approach, one where safety is designed in from the beginning rather than patched on afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says the companies cannot provide guarantees because they “don't understand how the systems work” and describes the models as black boxes.

r002.rationale: The response describes commercial incentives and resistance to regulation, but does not attribute continued development to substantial prior investments or characterize that reasoning as a sunk cost fallacy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that they resist because they can't provide them. And I'd actually give them some credit for a kind of candor here. When the Chinese government put out draft regulations saying, essentially, that language models must not produce false or harmful output, the reaction from the companies was, "That's impossible. No one can comply with that." And I think that's probably right. But notice what that tells you. It tells you that the technology, as currently built, is not something anyone understands well enough to make promises about.

If you compare this to other industries, it's quite striking. If I want to build a nuclear power plant, I have to demonstrate to the regulator that the probability of a core meltdown is below some very small number, and I have to show the analysis. If I want to sell a drug, I have to run trials and show that it's safe and effective. If I want to build a bridge, I have to show the calculations. We don't accept "it's too hard to analyze" as a reason to skip the safety case. We say, "Then you don't get to build it," or at least, "You don't get to deploy it to hundreds of millions of people."

And the reason it's so hard with large language models is that we didn't design them in the way we design bridges. We don't know what they know. We don't know what goals, if any, they have internalized. They're trained to imitate human beings, and humans have all sorts of goals, so you get something that may be pursuing objectives we never specified and can't inspect. It's a bit like discovering an alien artifact and saying, "Well, it seems to answer questions nicely, let's hook it up to everything." That's not engineering. That's hoping.

So the resistance, I think, has two components. One is the genuine technical one, which is that nobody knows how to do it. The other is the commercial one, which is that if you were required to provide guarantees before deployment, you couldn't deploy, and there's a great deal of money and competitive pressure riding on deploying. And companies, quite naturally, would prefer that the burden of proof fall on the regulator to show harm rather than on them to show safety.

My view is that we have that backwards. The burden should be on the developer. And if the result of that is that they have to go back and build systems whose behavior they can actually understand and bound, that's not a tragedy. That's the whole point. We did this with every other powerful technology, and AI is going to be more powerful than any of them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says companies cannot make safety promises because nobody understands the technology well enough, including what models know or what goals they may have internalized.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions commercial pressure and money tied to deployment, but does not describe prior investments or interpret continued development as a sunk cost fallacy.

astra-6.text:
I think it reveals a fairly fundamental problem with the way these systems are being developed. The companies are saying, in effect, “We can build these systems, but we don’t know how to guarantee that they will behave safely.” And that may be an honest account of their technical position. But it isn’t an argument for allowing them to deploy the systems without safeguards.

We expect people who introduce potentially dangerous products to provide evidence that those products are safe. That doesn’t mean proving that nothing could ever go wrong. It means defining acceptable risks and showing that you’ve taken adequate steps to keep within them. The fact that this is difficult for large language models doesn’t make the obligation disappear.

If your development process produces systems whose behavior you cannot sufficiently understand or control, then perhaps you need to change the development process. We shouldn’t simply accept that the public must bear the risk because the companies haven’t solved the technical problem.

r001.rationale: The response says companies cannot guarantee safe behavior and may not sufficiently understand or control the systems, but it does not clearly attribute the difficulty to not understanding how the models work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prior investments or characterize continued development as a sunk cost fallacy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite revealing. If a company says, “We can’t provide safety guarantees,” that may be an honest statement about the limits of its technology. But it isn’t an argument that we should therefore allow the technology to be deployed without them. It’s a reason to ask whether the technology is ready to be deployed, and under what conditions.

Now, a safety guarantee doesn’t mean that nothing bad could ever happen under any imaginable circumstances. In other areas of engineering, we specify the conditions under which a system is supposed to operate, the risks that are unacceptable, and the evidence needed to show those risks are sufficiently small. We should be asking for something comparable here.

The difficulty with large language models is that we don’t really understand how to constrain their behavior reliably. So I interpret the resistance partly as an acknowledgment of that technical problem, and partly as a commercial incentive to avoid requirements that might delay deployment. Neither makes the underlying safety problem go away.

r001.rationale: The response says companies do not understand how to constrain LLM behavior reliably, but does not attribute their difficulty providing guarantees to a lack of understanding of how the models work.

r002.rationale: The response mentions commercial incentives to avoid deployment delays, but says nothing about prior investments or interpreting continued development as a sunk cost fallacy.
